news.title: Who is Chris Van Hollen and why is he challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader?
news.description: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced this week that he will challenge Democratic stalwart Chuck Schumer of New York for Senate majority leader, setting up an internal clash over the direction of the party just days after its landslide victory in this year’s midterm elections. “We saw a huge outburst of democracy on Election Day — red states, blue states, purple states — and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty,” Van Hollen told MS NOW. “It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people. The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.” Van Hollen, 67, insisted that his decision was “not about any one person.” Yet progressives have long criticized the 75-year-old Schumer — who has served in the Senate since 1999 and led the Democratic caucus since 2017 — for what they characterize as his cautious, centrist approach to politics. Seven newly elected Democratic senators have already declined to support Schumer’s return as majority leader, a post he previously occupied from 2021 to 2025: Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, James Talarico of Texas, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire and Juliana Stratton of Illinois. On Tuesday, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, also said he would “not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader.” “If this campaign was about anything, it was about change, and the need for the Democratic Party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction,” Sanders told reporters. So who is Van Hollen, why is he challenging Schumer and does he really have a chance? Here’s everything you need to know about the intraparty battle that’s brewing ahead of next year’s Democratic takeover on Capitol Hill. Who is Chris Van Hollen? Van Hollen served seven terms in the House representing Maryland’s 8th Congressional District, a deep blue region mostly comprising the Washington, D.C., suburbs, before being elected to the Senate in 2016. He previously served as the head of the Democratic Party’s campaign committees for both the House and the Senate, roles that gave him a major influence on Democrats’ election strategy. In those roles, he helped oversee so-called blue wave elections in 2008 and 2018, but was also at the helm during the “shellacking” the party suffered at the hands of Republicans in 2010. Van Hollen is a progressive Democrat who has said he supports Medicare for All, raising the federal minimum wage and LGBTQ rights. In his bid for majority leader, he has the backing of two of the Senate’s most prominent progressive figures in Sanders and El-Sayed. In recent years, Van Hollen has been particularly critical of the U.S. relationship with Israel, including calling what he viewed as former President Joe Biden’s inaction on the war in Gaza “shameful.” More recently, he voted in favor of cancelling billions of dollars in weapons sales to Israel and introduced a bill aimed at investigating alleged human rights abuses in Palestine's West Bank. Van Hollen gained national attention in April 2025, when he travelled to El Salvador to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been wrongfully deported and sent to a notoriously brutal prison in the country. While Van Hollen sits to the ideological left of Schumer on some key policy issues, his main critique of the Democrats’ current leader in the Senate centers mostly on his approach. In his announcing his bid for majority leader, Van Hollen said Democrats “need to meet the moment with a bold agenda” — phrasing that suggests he doesn’t believe Schumer will be aggressive enough to take full advantage of the party’s power in Congress. What’s at stake Unlike the speaker of the House, the Senate majority leader isn’t mentioned in the Constitution. But over time it has evolved into one of the most powerful positions in Washington. By controlling which policies are emphasized, which bills are brought to the floor, when votes occur, which judges and appointees are confirmed and how all of this is communicated to the president and the public, majority leaders can effectively reshape the party — at least on a legislative level — in their image. They can also help recruit and fund Senate candidates for future elections. Schumer’s critics say his image is no longer a good match for the moment. Some have called for generational or cultural change. Some have insisted on geographic diversity, noting that both Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to be the next House speaker, represent New York. (They live about 15 minutes from each other in Brooklyn.) Some have demanded a more combative approach to the defining issues of the 2026 midterms: lowering the cost of living, ending the war in Iran, confronting the Trump administration. And some say they are simply seeking a conversation rather than a “coronation.” “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitively different,” Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a relative moderate, said Tuesday at a news conference with Sanders, leaving the door open to a leadership change. “What they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then, in particular, how they’re going to communicate differently.” Van Hollen has yet to articulate a concrete agenda. But earlier this week he criticized Schumer, who is Jewish, for his ties to Israel and other special interests, saying that the New York senator and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee “sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC,” the pro-Israel lobbying group, against Democratic candidates who went on to win the general election, including El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine. Van Hollen added that the DSCC should not take money from AIPAC in the future. Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, but he has strongly criticized outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza. Van Hollen has also argued that Democrats should refuse to pass any bill to fund the government unless it includes language to end the war in Iran, even if that leads to another government shutdown next month. “Right now, under our current leadership, we have a situation where they are not willing to use the most important power we have to end the war, which is to defund it,” he said Friday. What’s next House Speaker is chosen by a vote of the full chamber. But Senate majority leaders are selected by only one party in a secret, closed-door vote, which means much of the process leading up to Democrats’ leadership decision may happen out of the public eye. The vote is reportedly scheduled to take place on Dec. 1, but Politico reports that there have been discussions about moving it up to as soon as next week. Sen. Brian Schatz, a Democrat from Hawaii, urged his party to resolve its leadership dispute as soon as possible. “We must move quickly to vote, unify and get to work,” Schatz told the New York Times. It remains to be seen whether Van Hollen can collect the support of enough Democratic senators to present a true threat to Schumer’s leadership. On Thursday night, Schumer expressed confidence that he would overcome Van Hollen’s challenge. “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote on social media. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.” Some moderate senators have stepped forward to back Schumer, including Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman and Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats. After crediting Schumer with Democrats’ dominant performance in the midterms, King compared the situation to baseball. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” he asked. news.title: Our Revolution Endorses Chris Van Hollen for Senate Majority Leader
news.description: Our Revolution, the nation’s largest grassroots progressive organization endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader and urged Senate Democrats to vote for him over Sen. Chuck Schumer. The endorsement builds on the organization’s ongoing grassroots campaign to replace Schumer and secure an open, competitive leadership election. “Working people organized to win this majority, and they expect it to fight for them,” said Joseph Geevarghese, Executive Director of Our Revolution. “To be a real opposition party, Democrats have to take on corporate power, including the big donors and party insiders who stand in the way of change. That means getting corporate money out of politics, ending U.S. military aid to Israel, and fighting to pass Medicare for All. That’s the working-class agenda we’ve been organizing for, and it’s why we’ve called on Chuck Schumer to step aside. Chris Van Hollen has stepped up to challenge the status quo, and we’re urging Senate Democrats to vote for him.” In Our Revolution’s November 6–7 survey of 4,308 progressive respondents, 72% wanted new Senate leadership, 22% said it depended on whether Schumer delivers, and 5% supported his continued leadership. The results reflect participating respondents and are not representative of all Democratic voters. Our Revolution is asking supporters to sign the petition calling on Senate Democrats to replace Schumer.

news.title: House To Consider Preventive Care Savings Bill Under Suspension Of Rules
news.description: Body: The House will consider a bipartisan bill under suspension of the rules next week that would allow the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) to estimate the costs and savings of preventive health legislation over 30 years, rather than the current 10-year window. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise announced Friday (Nov. 13) that the House will consider the Preventive Health Savings Act (H.R. 4464) under suspension of the rules during the week of Nov. 16. The bill -- sponsored by Reps. Scott Peters (D-CA), Jay Obernolte (R-CA), Diana DeGette (D-CO) and Buddy Carter (R-GA) -- would allow lawmakers to ask CBO for a longer-term analysis of certain preventive-health legislation. If CBO determined the bill could produce net savings after the usual 10-year period, the agency would provide estimates for two additional 10-year periods. These additional estimates would only be supplemental and could not be used as offsets. The bill also defines preventive health care as interventions intended to prevent disease, disability and premature death. The House Budget Committee unanimously advanced the Preventive Health Savings Act in September, with no amendments offered. During the markup, Peters argued the bill would allow for more investment in preventive care, as well as increased savings. “Screening that catches cancer at stage one instead of stage four, a diabetes program that keeps someone off dialysis 15 years from now, a vaccine that prevents a hospitalization that would have happened decades from now -- these are investments we can make that will help sick patients and generate real cost savings down the road,” Peters said. An earlier version, led by former Rep. Michael Burgess (R-TX) and DeGette, passed the House during the 118th Congress but stalled in the Senate. And the Senate has not acted on its companion bill introduced this Congress from Sens. Angus King (I-ME), Mike Crapo (R-ID), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and Kevin Cramer (R-ND). -- Sigi Ris (sris@iwpnews.com)

news.title: Who is Chris Van Hollen and why is he challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader?
news.description: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced this week that he will challenge Democratic stalwart Chuck Schumer of New York for Senate majority leader, setting up an internal clash over the direction of the party just days after its landslide victory in this year’s midterm elections. “We saw a huge outburst of democracy on Election Day — red states, blue states, purple states — and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty,” Van Hollen told MS NOW. “It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people. The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.” Van Hollen, 67, insisted that his decision was “not about any one person.” Yet progressives have long criticized the 75-year-old Schumer — who has served in the Senate since 1999 and led the Democratic caucus since 2017 — for what they characterize as his cautious, centrist approach to politics. Seven newly elected Democratic senators have already declined to support Schumer’s return as majority leader, a post he previously occupied from 2021 to 2025: Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, James Talarico of Texas, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire and Juliana Stratton of Illinois. On Tuesday, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, also said he would “not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader.” “If this campaign was about anything, it was about change, and the need for the Democratic Party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction,” Sanders told reporters. So who is Van Hollen, why is he challenging Schumer and does he really have a chance? Here’s everything you need to know about the intraparty battle that’s brewing ahead of next year’s Democratic takeover on Capitol Hill. Who is Chris Van Hollen? Van Hollen served seven terms in the House representing Maryland’s 8th Congressional District, a deep blue region mostly comprising the Washington, D.C., suburbs, before being elected to the Senate in 2016. He previously served as the head of the Democratic Party’s campaign committees for both the House and the Senate, roles that gave him a major influence on Democrats’ election strategy. In those roles, he helped oversee so-called blue wave elections in 2008 and 2018, but was also at the helm during the “shellacking” the party suffered at the hands of Republicans in 2010. Van Hollen is a progressive Democrat who has said he supports Medicare for All, raising the federal minimum wage and LGBTQ rights. In his bid for majority leader, he has the backing of two of the Senate’s most prominent progressive figures in Sanders and El-Sayed. In recent years, Van Hollen has been particularly critical of the U.S. relationship with Israel, including calling what he viewed as former President Joe Biden’s inaction on the war in Gaza “shameful.” More recently, he voted in favor of cancelling billions of dollars in weapons sales to Israel and introduced a bill aimed at investigating alleged human rights abuses in Palestine's West Bank. Van Hollen gained national attention in April 2025, when he travelled to El Salvador to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been wrongfully deported and sent to a notoriously brutal prison in the country. While Van Hollen sits to the ideological left of Schumer on some key policy issues, his main critique of the Democrats’ current leader in the Senate centers mostly on his approach. In his announcing his bid for majority leader, Van Hollen said Democrats “need to meet the moment with a bold agenda” — phrasing that suggests he doesn’t believe Schumer will be aggressive enough to take full advantage of the party’s power in Congress. What’s at stake Unlike the speaker of the House, the Senate majority leader isn’t mentioned in the Constitution. But over time it has evolved into one of the most powerful positions in Washington. By controlling which policies are emphasized, which bills are brought to the floor, when votes occur, which judges and appointees are confirmed and how all of this is communicated to the president and the public, majority leaders can effectively reshape the party — at least on a legislative level — in their image. They can also help recruit and fund Senate candidates for future elections. Schumer’s critics say his image is no longer a good match for the moment. Some have called for generational or cultural change. Some have insisted on geographic diversity, noting that both Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to be the next House speaker, represent New York. (They live about 15 minutes from each other in Brooklyn.) Some have demanded a more combative approach to the defining issues of the 2026 midterms: lowering the cost of living, ending the war in Iran, confronting the Trump administration. And some say they are simply seeking a conversation rather than a “coronation.” “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitively different,” Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a relative moderate, said Tuesday at a news conference with Sanders, leaving the door open to a leadership change. “What they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then, in particular, how they’re going to communicate differently.” Van Hollen has yet to articulate a concrete agenda. But earlier this week he criticized Schumer, who is Jewish, for his ties to Israel and other special interests, saying that the New York senator and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee “sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC,” the pro-Israel lobbying group, against Democratic candidates who went on to win the general election, including El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine. Van Hollen added that the DSCC should not take money from AIPAC in the future. Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, but he has strongly criticized outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza. Van Hollen has also argued that Democrats should refuse to pass any bill to fund the government unless it includes language to end the war in Iran, even if that leads to another government shutdown next month. “Right now, under our current leadership, we have a situation where they are not willing to use the most important power we have to end the war, which is to defund it,” he said Friday. What’s next House Speaker is chosen by a vote of the full chamber. But Senate majority leaders are selected by only one party in a secret, closed-door vote, which means much of the process leading up to Democrats’ leadership decision may happen out of the public eye. The vote is reportedly scheduled to take place on Dec. 1, but Politico reports that there have been discussions about moving it up to as soon as next week. Sen. Brian Schatz, a Democrat from Hawaii, urged his party to resolve its leadership dispute as soon as possible. “We must move quickly to vote, unify and get to work,” Schatz told the New York Times. It remains to be seen whether Van Hollen can collect the support of enough Democratic senators to present a true threat to Schumer’s leadership. On Thursday night, Schumer expressed confidence that he would overcome Van Hollen’s challenge. “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote on social media. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.” Some moderate senators have stepped forward to back Schumer, including Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman and Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats. After crediting Schumer with Democrats’ dominant performance in the midterms, King compared the situation to baseball. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” he asked.
